title: CDC shifts newborn hepatitis B vaccine guidance to individual decision-making
description_medium: On December 16, 2025, the CDC adopted individual-based decision-making for hepatitis B vaccination of infants born to mothers who test negative for the virus. Parents and clinicians can decide whether to give the birth dose or begin later; if they defer it, the series should start no earlier than age two months. Infants whose mothers test positive or whose status is unknown should still receive vaccine within 12 hours of birth.
description_long: On December 16, 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention adopted individual-based decision-making for hepatitis B vaccination of infants born to mothers who test negative for the virus. Parents and health-care providers may decide together whether to give the birth dose or begin the series later in infancy; if the birth dose is deferred, the CDC suggests starting no earlier than two months of age. The recommendation followed a vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and changed the longstanding universal birth-dose guidance for infants in this group. The prior routine schedule began at birth, continued at one to two months, and placed the third dose between six and eighteen months. Infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose status is unknown remain on a different path: the CDC says they should receive the birth dose within 12 hours. The policy change concerns when and how parents and clinicians decide to vaccinate lower-risk infants; it does not remove the vaccine from the schedule or make it unavailable. The CDC said it was still reviewing the committee’s separate suggestion about antibody testing to decide whether later doses are needed.

corrected_wording.claim: The earlier batch gave the prior third-dose range as six to fifteen months.
corrected_wording.wording: The 2025 CDC schedule and guidance give the routine third-dose range as six to eighteen months. The CNN-syndicated account used for the original description says six to fifteen months; this amendment corrects that figure against CDC guidance.

source_access_notes: CDC’s 2025 immunization schedule and perinatal guidance were checked and support the 6–18 month routine third-dose range. The supplied Trump File page links a CNN account; a CNN Newsource syndication was accessible, and it gives a conflicting 6–15 month range. The correction follows CDC primary guidance.
rationale: Append-only factual amendment corrects the prior schedule’s third-dose age range and replaces evidence-audit prose with the policy details and exceptions documented in CDC guidance.
